According to [4], this scenario occurs when T2 and its server, 82, are released at the same time, their effect can have significant, and even adverse impact on the schedulability of a system. To the best of our knowledge, no RTA exists for systems scheduled by fixed priority servers in a HFPP setting that considers the effect of overheads.

Thus, this work makes the following contributions: (i) We present an overhead-aware method to assess the schedulability of real-time applications in a HFPP setting, and (ii) show their influence on system schedulability. (iii) We also show how an existing sufficient, but not necessary, study [4] is inadequate for server parameter selection in hierarchical settings, and (iv) based on the proposed overhead model, we derive a practical parameter selection heuristic that results in schedulable systems with low utilization and small WCRTs.

The paper is structured as follows. Section II discuss our motivation. Sections III and IV present the task and demandsupply model respectively. Section V presents the exact overhead-oblivious RTA that in combination with the overhead model of Section VI lay the foundation for the overhead-aware analysis presented in Section VII. While Section VIII proposes an optimal parametrization technique, Section IX details our experimental evaluation. Section X concludes the paper.

div.head: II. MOTIVATION
div.p: Even though the overheads induced by the implementation of a given server algorithm can have a negative impact on the schedulability of a system, all of the preceding analysis, either neglect their dimensions [6], [7], or provide simplistic approaches to account for them [4]. Moreover, regarding the optimal server parameter selection, studies using methods based on RTAs that are only necessary but not sufficient, such as [4], can lead to wrong conclusions as shown in the next example. Consider the Deferrable Servers 81 and 82 (Table I [Right]), scheduling the tasks shown in Table I [Left]. Moreover, assume 81 has the highest priority.

Abstract-Real-time servers have been widely explored in the scheduling literature to predictably execute aperiodic activities, as well as to allow hierarchical scheduling settings. As they allow achieving timing isolation between previously isolated and functionally diverse applications, there is a renewed interest for the adoption of fixed priority real-time servers in the automotive domain, as a way to implement more efficient reservation mechanisms than TDMA-based methods. Thus, this paper presents an overhead-aware schedulability analysis for hierarchical fixed priority preemptive (HFPP) systems, and proposes a practical server parameterization technique preserving the least possible utilization and enhancing the aggregated WCRT, i.e. the sum of WCRTs, of the tasks in a hierarchical scheduling setting.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION AND RELATED WORK
div.p: Although, initially conceived as a way to deal with dualcriticality systems, in [1], the use of servers was extended to deal with hierarchical scheduling systems, where a number of separate applications are assigned to the same processor, and each application is scheduled through a dedicated server. Each server may have a different (local) scheduler, while the servers are scheduled globally on the considered processor.

The compositional timing guarantees provided by serverbased systems are of particular interest to the automotive domain, where different SW components may be concurrently executed on the same platform. However, the OSEK-AUTOSAR standard does not propose any application programming interface to implement compositional scheduling by means of servers. Despite existing practices in the automotive and avionic domain where Time Division Multiple Access (TDMA) approaches are adopted to provide temporal isolation among different applications, there has been a growing interest in rt servers as an alternative method to obtain better results.

While tight upper bounds on the response time analyses for jobs scheduled in hierarchical settings have been derived [2], [3], [4], [5], it was only recently that in [6], [7] the authors presented an exact response time analysis (RTA) that, unlike its predecessors, does not require a critical instant, i.e. the pattern of execution of other tasks and servers leading to the worst-case response time (WCRT) of a task. Finding such a worst-case scenario, as exposed in [5], is not trivial at all. However, while these works consider overheads as negligible, but the execution of the server is delayed due to interference from Sl. This example and the experiments of Section IX show that existing studies of the optimal server parameter selection for HFPP systems are inconclusive and that such an investigation can only be built on an exact overhead-aware analysis.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: We assume a system composed of tasks and servers scheduled according to a fixed priority preemptive policy, where a server can host multiple tasks. Each task Ti consists of a stream of jobs, Ji,j, characterized by an arrival time ai,j, a start time Si,j, a finishing time Ii,j, and a computation time Ci,j. Moreover, each periodic task Ti is characterized by a tuple (T i , C i , D i ), where T i is its period, C i = maXj{ci,j} its worst-case execution time (WCET), and D i its deadline. Unless otherwise stated, deadlines are implicit, i.e D i = T i . The utilization of a task, U i , is the ratio of its WCET to its period, i.e. U i = Ci/T i . Furthermore, a server S is characterized by a tuple (T s , C s ), where T s is its period and C s its capacity or budget. The budget is replenished according to a bandwidth-preserving fixed priority server algorithm such as the Deferrable Server (DS) [8]. The utilization of a server, Us, is the quotient of its budget and its period, i.e. Us = Cs/T s , and Us represents the aggregated utilization of its tasks, i.e. Us = L: U i Vi in s. The hyperperiod, is the least common multiple (LCM) of all servers and tasks' periods.

div.head: VI. OVERHEAD MODEL
div.p: To integrate overhead accounting into the presented schedulability analysis, we modeled overheads by inflating the demand, i.e. the execution requirement, of a task. Notice that this work deals with context-switch and scheduling overhead. While the former refers to the overhead due to task switching, the latter is the overhead associated to task selection. Overheads due to the execution of an interrupt (release and handling), as well as cache-related overheads are not considered in this paper. Henceforth context-switch and scheduling overheads are referred to as overheads.

In a HFPPS, overheads manifest themselves when a job is preempted by a higher priority job. In such a case, the costs of a preemption are charged to the preempting higher priority job. In this way, the execution requirement of each job is inflated at its release and on its completion by adding the maximum worst-case overhead, i.e. the maximum duration of the combination of a context-switch and scheduling overhead, in each case. Automotive applications are particularly concerned with optimizing end-to-end propagation latencies of input events that trigger a chain of computations, leading to a final actuation [9]. As this optimization involves reducing the aggregated WCRT of tasks in a given system, we aim at providing an optimal set of server parameters that leads to a schedulable system with minimal processor utilization as well as small aggregated WCRT.

Based on the overhead model presented in this article, we can draw the following conclusion: If for each server 8 in a given system, its period, T s , is the LCM of its associated tasks, i.e. T s = LCM{Td \i task Ti in 8, and its budget, C s , is equal to T s ' L:(C i +2CO)/T i \i task Ti in 8, and the system is schedulable, then the server parametrization is optimal in terms of utilization. By deploying this server parameter selection, the execution demand of each job of a given task is only inflated by 2Co, since there is no overhead induced due to an extra release or budget exhaustion of its server. As shown in the following section, this parametrization indeed produces schedulable systems with minimum utilization and small aggregated WCRT.

div.head: IX. EVALUATION
div.p: Having established an overhead model for HFPPSs, and its corresponding RTA, we hereafter provide an experimental study of the server parameter selection. For each experiment, where synthetic tasks are generated, task and server periods are constrained to ensure that the hyperperiod does not exceed 30 seconds, as each task set was run for this time.

div.head: A. Analysis methods without overheads
div.p: In order to assess how well [4] and [6], [7] deal with the problem of finding the optimal set of server parameters, an exhaustive search based on these analysis is carried out. To that end, consider the system described in Table IV, where the DS 81 has a higher priority than that of the DS 82. For the sake Furthermore, let the tuple (C SJ T s ) represent the parameters of a server 8, then the optimal set of parameters given by [6], [7] is (2,10) and (14,50) for 81 and 82 (as depicted in the inset), respectively, with a CPU utilization of 0.48 and an aggregation of 13. The aggregated WCRT and the utilization are the smallest possible numbers in the experiment. Nevertheless, with these parameters [4] claims that the system is not schedulable. It even suggests (1,5) and (3,10) as optimal parameters for 81 and 82 (refer to the figure), respectively, with a system utilization of 0.5 and aggregation of 33, provided that minimizing the utilization prevails over a minimization of the aggregated WCRT. Otherwise, it proposes (1,5) and (4,5) as optimal parameters for the highest and lowest (as shown in the picture) priority servers, respectively, with a system utilization of 1 and aggregation of 17. For the set of parameters of the first and second case, [6], [7] provide an aggregated WCRT of 24 and 15, respectively, confirming the pessimism of [4].

In conclusion, while the analysis presented in [4] is not suited for a thorough study of the server parameter selection problem for HFPPSs, its main advantage is its simplicity to compute upper bounds on the response time of tasks.

div.head: B. Effect of overheads
div.p: As existing methods, such as [4], do not consider the effects of overheads in their analysis, the preceding comparison was made ignoring their effect. Thus, in order to present a more realistic study, the next experiment aims at showing the effects of an overhead-aware exact analysis. For this reason, consider the system of Table IV once more and assume that the maximum worst-case overhead is 0.1, i.e. Co = 0.1. Conducting the same exhaustive search described in the previous experiment produces the results shown in Figure 4.

First of all, Fig. 4 (Left) makes evident that the number of feasible parameter sets decreases. In fact, it drops to 5999, i.e. the effect of overheads leads to a 58.66% reduction in the number of schedulable systems in comparison to that obtained by an overhead-agnostic schedulability analysis. It can also be seen that the amount of parameter sets resulting in a large aggregated WCRT increases as indicated by the darker color of the dots. Recall that the aggregated WCRT is color encoded and different values for the same pair of parameters of 82 are superimposed, which can be better appreciated in the corresponding 3D scatter plot (Fig. 4 (Right». In Fig. 3 each dot represents the aggregated WCRT, with the horizontal and vertical position showing the period and budget of 82. Moreover, the aggregation is encoded by color, where a smaller value is reflected in a lighter color. As the aggregated WCRT depends not only on the parameters of the lowest priority server but also on those of 81, when the same pair of parameters of 82 yields different results, their encoded colors are superimposed. The inset only displays pairs that produce a schedulable system. Furthermore, the figure shows a comparison between results obtained by means of [6], [7] (Left) against those through the method in [4] (Right).

As expected, the scatter plots show a positive correlation between the budget and the period for both analysis, as increasing the period results in a proportional increment in the budget. Moreover, since the analysis proposed in [4] is based on a critical instant that does not necessarily occur, this pessimism manifests itself in the lower number of schedulable systems as shown by the number of dots in the figure, as well as the fact that all obtained parameters are a subset of the ones produced by the analysis in [6], [7]. Indeed, while use of [6], [7] produces 10227 schedulable systems, deployment of [4] only makes for 364, i.e. 3.56%, of the actual number.

div.head: C. Server parameter selection
div.p: To show that the server parameter selection proposed in Section VIII can indeed produce optimal results, we synthetically produce task sets based on an industrial case study consisting of an automotive engine control system [10]. Hence, we generate task sets ranging from 3 to 9 tasks, where tasks' periods are randomly chosen with uniform distribution from {I, 2, 5, 10,20,50, 100,200, 1000}ms, and randomly assigned to servers. The number of servers ranges from 1 to 6 and the number of task sets is 70.

In this experiment, we distinguish between two kinds of parametrization. The first method is derived from Section VIII, where the period, T s , and budget, C s , of a server s, are computed as T s = LCM{Td, and C s = T s •L-(C i +2•CO)/T i \I task Ti in the server. The maximum worst-case overhead, Co, is obtained from measurements on the platform. The second parametrization involves randomly choosing the server's period and calculating its budget as C s = f3 . T s . Us, where f3 is randomly chosen within [1.2,1.3]. On the aforementioned platform, this f3 parameter proves to be overcompensating for the overhead involved. This process is repeated 100 times per task set to choose the best parameters. Fig. 5 (Left) shows the box plot of the aggregated WCRT in each set for both parametrizations. The inset depicts that the inter-quartile range, defined by the first quartile, Ql, and the third quartile, Q3, of the first method (Ql = 82.03, Q3 = 457.58) is lower than that of the other (Ql = 113.91, Q3 = 762.58). Moreover, the median (Q2 = 208.46) and maximum value (max = 836.99) of the random parametrization are much higher than those of its counterpart (Q2 = 153.61, max = 604.49). This indicates that the proposed parametrization indeed yields better results than a trial-and-error approach. Observe that this technique produces optimal results provided that the system is schedulable. In this experiment the suggested parametrization method resulted in 89% of the generated task sets being schedulable. Furthermore, even if optimizing the aggregated WCRT does not necessarily imply that each individual WCRT is minimal, the proposed parametrization can also address this problem and achieve good results as illustrated by Fig. 5 (Right).
